editorial:
Ever wonder how a simple joke on the internet can turn into a giant mess in the real world? You will get a front-row seat to that chaos here. The movie takes you back to the early days of the web where people just wanted to share funny images and trick each other with things like Rickrolling. It feels like a wild ride through a digital scrapbook, showing you how a group of bored people with too much time on their hands accidentally built a powerhouse of influence. The vibe is a mix of a history lesson and a true crime story, making you feel like you are uncovering a secret about how the world actually works today.

What really works is how the movie keeps things moving fast so you never get bored. The interviews are great, and the way they use old internet clips makes it feel authentic. One downside is that it covers a lot of ground, so some parts feel a bit rushed. Still, if you enjoy learning about the dark side of social media, you need to see this. For the best experience, try streaming it in 4K Ultra HD on Prime Video to see all those old screenshots clearly, or just rent it on Apple TV for a movie night with friends.
endingExplained: The movie wraps up by showing that the internet never really forgets anything. It explains that while the original pranksters moved on, the tools they created are now used by political groups to spread lies. The final scenes show how the line between a joke and a weapon has disappeared. It ends with a warning that the next big wave of online chaos is already starting, leaving you to wonder who is really in control.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves internet culture, tech history, and mysteries.
